Chase Noe, Griffin Rafferty, Meghan Sweeney, Xander Godar2

Hull Design
This section is split into three distinct sections: In-House Design, Market Options,
and Final Hull Customizations. The full justification for this organization will become
clearer as details in each section are disclosed, but in short, our initial evaluation made
clear that the best choice for a hull would be one that was designed in-house to our
specific needs. This decision is somewhat obvious before time & money are considered but
given the high personnel and budget cost of designing and fabricating a hull, it was a tough
choice. We reserved the idea of re-evaluating market options due to these costs and
moved forward with in-house design until it became clear that we would not be able to line
up manufacturers for our mold plug-in time. At that point, we went back to the drawing
board and looked at what could be bought to serve as our hull, eventually landing on a
whitewater kayak for a variety of reasons. This kayak, though, was not perfect, and thus we
decided to make some additional parts to fit the remaining needs.

displacement given additional payload, lack of optimization for speed, and difficulties with
waterlogging. Given this, one of the first things that we did was evaluate our general

Given the overall balance of complexity, stability, and drag, we decided on a vbottomed hull with stabilizers. This shape would offer a low drag thanks to the lift
generated by the fins and main shape alike and have a low chance of roll thanks to the drag
generated by lateral motion in regions of instantaneous change of slope (bottom edge,
fins). With that decided, several drafts were modeled in SolidWorks by the team, eventually
deciding on the following:
*Models show only the starboard side, port side was intended to be an exact mirroring of
the above7

This design was sufficiently hydrodynamic and aerodynamic to provide the least
drag as could be reasonably expected while providing enough displacement (120 lbs when
the waterline is 4 inches below the leading point of the hull) to allow for this and following
year’s weight requirements. This was determined through several drafts of models and
SolidWorks flow simulations which were used to determine high- and low-pressure points,
each of which was then targeted with the following model for ironing out.
With our finalized design in hand, we went looking for manufacturers. It was around
mid-December at that time, and we sent out feelers to several companies and people,
including wooden boat builders, wood furniture makers, and general carpenters. A week or
two later, we heard back one-by-one that they were unable to accommodate our project in
the timeline we needed, which, in hindsight, is something we should’ve expected. We
decided that rather than research more manufacturers and hope for them to have time in
their schedules, we would come together and re-define our needs to choose a marketavailable hull that would fit them best. In this process, we decided on a few of the most
important aspects: stability, drag, ease of retrofitting to watertightness, weight limit, and
internal space.

And so, for its size, stability, drag, cost, and water resistance, we chose a whitewater
kayak designed for a <120lb athlete. This weight limit allows for considerable expansion on
internals, so future years shouldn’t have to consider their hull unless they choose to. The
drag of a kayak is similar to what we would have had with our in-house hull, depending on
how much either would have lifted out of the water, its cost was only ~$1,300, which left
considerable room for electronics, and its small open area made for easy plans to design a
waterproofing solution. However, this option did leave us with one issue: as it has a flat
bottom, the kayak may be easy to capsize temporarily, which, though its self-righting may
fix, is still sub-ideal. Because of this, we decided that alongside thruster mounts, we would
design fins to largely rid ourselves of this problem using their large lateral drag coefficients.
Final Hull Customizations
For fins, we did not do anything extraordinary: fins have a fairly standard shape, and
so when modeling for our 3D print, we simply followed that design. That is, we followed it
until the idea to mount thrusters on the side of our fins was pitched. This change would
simplify our design process, reduce failure points, and allow for extra fin space if we
needed yet more stability. That led us to this 3D model*.
*3D model is accurate at the time of submission, but may be changed by competition, as
materials are cheap and readily available1011

Thrusters/Propulsion
The thrusters that were originally chosen for our boat were chosen to accommodate the
larger hull and more weight, as well as give the boat a general power advantage. We ran into late
issues with these thrusters and their compatibility with the Electronic Speed Controllers we
originally used. Unfortunately, with how late this happened and budget issues, the only choice
that we were left with was to reuse the thrusters from last year. The boat will be steered with
differential thrust to each thruster using an electronic speed controller connected to each motor.
Apisqueen AQ1020
The original thruster that was chosen was the Apisqueen AQ1020. As said above, this
thruster proved to be the most optimal for the setup that was first planned to run. Many things
have changed with the overall boat setup, which also now includes the thrusters. The AQ 1020
outputs 53 lbs of force at 50V, making it optimal to match with the batteries chosen and the
weight of the vessel. The major issue that was discovered was the non-compatibility with the
ESCs, causing us to switch. These thrusters came with a plastic mounting block as pictured
below. The thruster would have been mounted sideways on the fins that come off the bottom of
the boat. The benefits of this thruster are more power and a fully metal construction. The
downsides are the inability to connect with the current ESCs, questionable stability and the large
footprint leading to more drag.
*AQ1020 Thruster
Blue Robotics T500
The Blue Robotics T500 was the thruster package used by the 2023-24 PEP team at
Madison College. They chose this thruster due to it being light enough to fit on their boat and it
is an incredibly stable thruster. They also saw it is the best mix of power to the weight of the boat 12

as well as the mounting ease and small design. This thruster also is compatible with the
electronic speed controllers chosen for both last year and this current year. The T500 outputs
35.5 lbs of force at 24.4 volts. These thrusters are mounted sideways onto the fin, just as the
AQ1020 would have been. The benefits of this thruster are its smaller, more hydrodynamic
design, better stability, and less expensive. The downsides are some parts being made from
plastic and less power.
*T500 Thruster
There is a risk in running these thrusters that the much heavier weight of the boat will be
too much for the T500 thruster to handle in taller waves and currents. Based on the calculations
that have been done, on flat water the thrusters will propel the boat at an estimation of 6-8 mph,
not including outside drag from currents, waves, etc. Even with taller waves and currents, the
boat is expected to handle well due to the hull shape.
An issue that the 2024-25 team planned to address this year was achieving better water
flow to the thruster. The 2023-24 team had the thruster mounted too close to the bottom of the
hull making the water that flowed through the thruster would be very turbulent and the thrusters
wouldn’t be as efficient. They also mounted the thrusters on an object that was not
hydrodynamic. The updated version has the thrusters about 8 inches from the bottom of the hull
with a sleeker mounting system that doubles to keep the boat on track while driving. The
electrical cord for each thruster will follow the mounting fin up into the boat, to its ESC and
battery pack.13

Other Considered Options
One Thruster and Rutter
The team considered a few options before landing on the dual thruster set up with
differential thrust for steering. The main competitor to our option was a one-fixed thruster that
was far more powerful than the options we decided on. This system would be steered via rutter.
The downsides to this were the unreliability of a one-thruster set up compared to a two-thruster
set up should one fail and the rutter is a very complicated part when considering how to make it
stable and effective. Overall, the two-thruster system had far more positives than the one-thruster
system.
Rotating Thruster
The other choice we liked was having one or two thrusters that could rotate to steer. This system
would have been very similar to a trolling motor on a fishing boat. We soon realized while
looking into this type of system that it would not be the best option. The big issues are trying to
find a rotating thruster or finding a way to rotate a thruster from its fixed point. We couldn’t find
enough information on this outside of trolling motors which are not allowed under the
competition rules.
Power System
From the previous year's power system, we inherited roughly 98 18650 Li-ion battery
cells. Due to the success of the previous team and the high energy density and lower cost of Liion batteries, we decided to use the same battery chemistry to build two identical battery packs,
one for each thruster. In addition, the cells we are using have BMS protection which limits the
current output and will protect the battery from short circuits.
Despite the fact that we had inherited usable batteries, the old cells were not ideal
or completely safe to use. Once the battery was disassembled each cell was at a different voltage.
Because of this, it was unsafe to spot-weld the cells in parallel, as that can lead to overheating in
the battery, damaging it. We found it better to buy new cells to reduce risk, so we bought new
Samsung 30Q18650 batteries.
We had hoped to initially build a battery with 12 cells in series and 8 in parallel. This
would make each battery have a total voltage of 44.4V and a capacity of 24Ah. This system had
ideal power for our original thrusters, which ran on 48V. However, due to our need to change the
thrusters and use our inherited thruster, our battery design had to change. The battery now had to
be designed to have a maximum voltage of 24V, so our final battery layout includes 6 cells in
series and 8 cells in parallel. This battery layout also provides a larger variety of options for ESC
and chargers, while still allowing us to increase the capacity if needed. 14

The final voltage of our battery is 22.2V with a capacity of 24Ah. The cells are aligned
with spacers and are spot-welded together with 0.15mm nickel strips. The welded battery is
wrapped in rubber sheets which will help in reducing the vibration of the cells, then wrapped in
heat shrink to form a solid package. After charging to their full capacity, the batteries will be
mounted to the boat inside of a waterproof box.
Control System
Our control system uses the MT12 surface radio made by Radio Master as the transmitter and the
receiver we used is the ER5C-1 channel receiver by the same manufacturer. The RadioMaster
MT12 is the first open-source surface radio to officially be supported by EdgeTX, ExpressLRS,
and the Multi-module project. With 10 physical inputs and the capability to handle up to 32
channels, the MT12 can handle a wide array of surface models, from cars and trucks to boats and
beyond. Due to its extensive customizability, the MT12 is prepared to excel in almost every
scenario, making it the obvious choice for our boat control system.
Project Conclusion
This project was definitely a new experience for all of us. We didn’t have a great idea of
where to start on this project and when we did start we had a lot of waiting for responses.
We definitely got into a time jam on this project but we learned a great deal from being
thrown into the fire. We hope that future groups can learn from our mistakes and keep
creating better boats down the road.15

Acknowledgments
Our project has been a great learning experience for the team in all aspects of
engineering and we are greatly appreciative to be a part of the ASNE PEP program to help
further our knowledge of electric propulsion. Our team wants to thank Michael Briscoe and
the ASNE for making this opportunity possible. The Madison College STEM Center and its
employees Carolyn Kosabucki, Tom Fleming, and Levi Lee have been incredible in their
help and dedication to the success of this year's team. We cannot give enough thanks to
everyone involved in this project and making it a reality.

From the previous year's power system, we inherited roughly 98 18650 Li-ion battery
cells. Due to the success of the previous team and the high energy density and lower cost of Liion batteries, we decided to use the same battery chemistry to build two identical battery packs,
one for each thruster. In addition, the cells we are using have BMS protection which limits the
current output and will protect the battery from short circuits.
Despite the fact that we had inherited usable batteries, the old cells were not ideal
or completely safe to use. Once the battery was disassembled each cell was at a different voltage.
Because of this, it was unsafe to spot-weld the cells in parallel, as that can lead to overheating in
the battery, damaging it. We found it better to buy new cells to reduce risk, so we bought new
We had hoped to initially build a battery with 12 cells in series and 8 in parallel. This
would make each battery have a total voltage of 44.4V and a capacity of 24Ah. This system had
ideal power for our original thrusters, which ran on 48V. However, due to our need to change the
thrusters and use our inherited thruster, our battery design had to change. The battery now had to
be designed to have a maximum voltage of 24V, so our final battery layout includes 6 cells in
series and 8 cells in parallel. This battery layout also provides a larger variety of options for ESC
and chargers, while still allowing us to increase the capacity if needed. 14
The final voltage of our battery is 22.2V with a capacity of 24Ah. The cells are aligned
with spacers and are spot-welded together with 0.15mm nickel strips. The welded battery is
wrapped in rubber sheets which will help in reducing the vibration of the cells, then wrapped in
heat shrink to form a solid package. After charging to their full capacity, the batteries will be
mounted to the boat inside of a waterproof box.
Our control system uses the MT12 surface radio made by Radio Master as the transmitter and the
receiver we used is the ER5C-1 channel receiver by the same manufacturer. The RadioMaster
MT12 is the first open-source surface radio to officially be supported by EdgeTX, ExpressLRS,
and the Multi-module project. With 10 physical inputs and the capability to handle up to 32
channels, the MT12 can handle a wide array of surface models, from cars and trucks to boats and
beyond. Due to its extensive customizability, the MT12 is prepared to excel in almost every
scenario, making it the obvious choice for our boat control system.
This project was definitely a new experience for all of us. We didn’t have a great idea of
where to start on this project and when we did start we had a lot of waiting for responses.
We definitely got into a time jam on this project but we learned a great deal from being
thrown into the fire. We hope that future groups can learn from our mistakes and keep
creating better boats down the road.15
